name: Drizzle
tagline: Slimmed-down MySQL fork rebuilt as a plugin microkernel for web and cloud workloads; abandoned since 2012.
description: Drizzle was a fork of the abandoned MySQL 6.0 development tree started by Brian Aker in 2008, with contributors from Sun, Rackspace and the wider MySQL community. It reorganised MySQL around a small C++ microkernel and pushed authentication (PAM, LDAP, HTTP auth), logging, replication, query caching, query rewriting and storage engines into plugins, dropped a good deal of MySQL legacy, and assumed POSIX systems, UTF-8 strings and MVCC transactions. The first GA release came in March 2011 and the last, 7.2.4, in September 2012; active development ended by late 2013 and the maintainers formally wound the project up in July 2016. It is not a database to deploy today, but its modularisation ideas show up in later MySQL, MariaDB and Percona work.
statusNote: Last release 7.2.4 in September 2012; maintainers formally wound the project up in July 2016. Use MySQL, MariaDB or Percona Server instead.

scale.notes: Single primary with plugin-based replication; sharding was left to the application.

strengths: Clean plugin microkernel: auth, logging, replication and engines were all swappable modules
Modern C++ codebase without MySQL's legacy baggage, useful for studying server design
Spoke the MySQL protocol, so existing clients could connect
weaknesses: No release since 2012 and no security fixes
Diverged from MySQL in features and behaviour, so existing applications rarely ran unmodified
Never gained the ecosystem, tooling or hosting support of MySQL forks that survived
useCases: Historical study of MySQL forks and modular server architecture
Reading plugin-API designs for database servers
notIdealFor: Applications that need MySQL feature parity
